puzzles.hint: What the cook leaves behind after the pickling is done — and what the ocean has in abundance.
puzzles.fact: Brine comes from an old Germanic root meaning “salt,” and it long referred both to salty water and to the liquid used for preserving food.
puzzles.intro: A salty little Wordle from the deep. Look for something the ocean has plenty of, but the clue is trying not to be too obvious.

puzzles.hint: What the mountain keeps under pressure, long before it has anything to say.
puzzles.fact: The word comes from Greek via Latin and originally referred to an unguent or thick paste before it became the molten rock beneath Earth’s crust.
puzzles.intro: A hot one from below: five letters, all pressure, no patience. See if you can name the stuff before it becomes a spectacle.

puzzles.hint: The sky’s bad mood, in five letters and one syllable.
puzzles.fact: Storm comes from Old English and shares roots with words for disturbance and tumult; it’s been a weather word for centuries, but also a metaphor for any sudden upheaval.
puzzles.intro: A little meteorology, a little mischief: solve the five-letter weather word from the clue. Keep an eye on the sky.

puzzles.hint: It brings the batter together without asking for credit.
puzzles.fact: ‘Mixer’ extends the ordinary idea of mixing into the kitchen, where the appliance turned a hand job into a powered one and became a staple of modern baking.
puzzles.intro: A room full of tools, smells, and half-finished intentions. See if you can land on the thing that fits the clue best.

puzzles.hint: A visitor with a tail, rarely punctual, and never signed to stay.
puzzles.fact: The word comes from Greek komētēs, meaning 'long-haired,' a nod to the glowing tail that made these objects seem star-like and wild to early observers.
puzzles.intro: A quick glance upward, and the clue might seem obvious—until it isn’t. Keep your eyes on the heavens and your guesses on earth.

puzzles.hint: A talkative import with a flair for imitating the neighbors.
puzzles.fact: The myna bird is famous for mimicry; some species can copy human speech, which is why it became a popular cage bird and a symbol of chatter.
puzzles.intro: A feathered five-letter answer is hiding here. Think less field guide, more sly clue.

puzzles.hint: Where the wheels keep their vows, and the game is always measured in pairs.
puzzles.fact: “Track” comes from the notion of a path or course, and on railways it became the standard word for the paired running surface that guides the wheels.
puzzles.intro: All aboard: a five-letter answer hides in the world of railways. Solve the clue, then ride the letters to the station.

puzzles.hint: A café order that also names a tan tone and a chocolatey dessert cousin.
puzzles.fact: The name comes from Mocha, the Yemeni port that long exported coffee to the world, and the term later broadened to describe coffee-and-chocolate flavors.
puzzles.intro: A cup, a roast, a buzz — something in that orbit is hiding here. The clue is indirect on purpose, so think café menu more than dictionary entry.

puzzles.hint: The card catalog’s old mastermind: it points you to everything else.
puzzles.fact: An index is a finding aid, and library indexes helped readers navigate collections long before search bars turned every shelf into a query.
puzzles.intro: A quiet place with a lot of hidden paths. Solve the five-letter word that belongs in the stacks.

puzzles.hint: The first white on the windshield, or the finishing touch on a cake.
puzzles.fact: Old English had this word as forst, and its twin life in weather and baking gives it a neat double meaning: the same look of white that can greet both a morning commute and a pastry case.
puzzles.intro: A cold-season Wordle: five letters, one wintry answer. The clue is meant to feel more like a little riddle than a definition.

puzzles.hint: What moviegoers used to unwind after a screening, and what a gossip-filled feed still gives you in snippets.
puzzles.fact: The word comes from the small cylinders that held early film stock; even after movies went digital, 'reel' stayed behind as a stubborn cinema fossil.
puzzles.intro: Lights down, eyes forward: this one lives somewhere between the marquee and the projector room. See if you can catch the word before the credits roll.

puzzles.hint: A living wall trimmed to a line, not bricks.
puzzles.fact: Hedges have long been used to mark boundaries and shelter garden beds; the word comes from Old English and is tied to the idea of enclosure.
puzzles.intro: Here’s a little five-letter puzzle rooted in the garden. Think of something that can shape a space without a shovel or stone.

puzzles.hint: The thing you strike when several notes decide to get along.
puzzles.fact: “Chord” comes via French from a musical sense of “agreement,” which is why it can still imply harmony or accord outside music.
puzzles.intro: A small music-themed Wordle: five letters, one answer. Listen for the clue, then see what fits.

puzzles.hint: A titan’s burden, if you’re looking for the book beside the globe.
puzzles.fact: The word comes from the Titan Atlas, who in Greek myth was imagined as bearing the heavens; map collections took his name in the 16th century and it stuck.
puzzles.intro: A cartographic little mystery: solve the five-letter word that fits the theme. Think of shelves, margins, and the thing that helps you orient the world.
